title: Denmark Ratifies Landmark Greenland Security Deal With U.S., Easing Transatlantic Tensions
snippet: Danish lawmakers unanimously approved a pivotal defense agreement with the United States regarding Greenland, seeking to de-escalate months of diplomatic friction over the strategic Arctic territory's future.
content:
COPENHAGEN — Danish lawmakers voted unanimously Thursday to ratify a major security agreement with the United States concerning Greenland, aiming to put an end to a tense diplomatic standoff over the strategic Arctic island's future.

The agreement, originally signed in September by representatives from the U.S., Denmark, and Greenland, follows months of friction within the NATO alliance after President Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the mineral-rich territory.

Expanding Military Presence and Missile Defense

Under the updated framework, the U.S. military will broaden its operational scope in Greenland, which includes permission to set up two new U.S. military bases and construct a 'Golden Dome' missile defense system. The treaty explicitly reaffirms Danish sovereignty over Greenland while guaranteeing the local population's right to self-determination.

"This agreement modernizes the United States-Denmark-Greenland defence partnership and bolsters the national security of the United States and our allies in NATO," U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in an official statement.

Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus indicated that the signatories will now draft a new legal framework to screen foreign investments in Greenland on national security grounds and finalize plans for the new U.S. installations.

Lingering Distrust and Resource Debates

Despite the parliamentary approval in both Greenland and Denmark, the high-pressure negotiations have strained relations. Naaja Nathanielsen, a Greenlandic member of the Danish parliament, acknowledged that Washington's aggressive push had bred deep mistrust among locals.

"It's been really difficult for Greenlanders these past two years. It's been seeping into every aspect of our lives," Nathanielsen said, expressing hope that the deal would help rebuild healthy transatlantic dialogue.

Friction may also persist over natural resources. President Trump recently claimed that major oil, gas, and mineral exploration projects were imminent. However, Greenland currently bans new crude oil drilling, and Danish authorities emphasized that any future mining or energy projects must adhere strictly to local law.

Foreign policy analysts note that while the treaty provides immediate stability, it grants Washington significantly more leverage over security and strategic resource extraction in the Arctic moving forward.
